clue.text: Delights of the daily paper

parts.note: a daily, in British usage, is a cleaning lady, also called a char
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a paper document

explanation.surface: The pleasures to be found in reading one's morning newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The daily paper' reads as a newspaper, but 'daily' is the British word for a cleaner (a char), and 'paper' is a manuscript.
explanation.definitionFit: Charms are things that please or enchant, just as delights are.

clue.text: Eccentric writer encloses money for a shrub

parts.note: a cam is an eccentric wheel in machinery

indicators.note: the writer's name wraps round the money

parts.note: Elia was the pen name of the essayist Charles Lamb
L stands for libra, the pound sterling

explanation.surface: An oddball author tucks cash inside a bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like an adjective for the writer, but it is a noun: a cam, an off-centre wheel. 'for a' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The camellia is an evergreen flowering bush from East Asia.

clue.text: Order nearly all tropical fruit

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, so these letters are rearranged
the whole word but its last letter is used

explanation.surface: A customer requests almost the whole range of exotic produce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly all' drops the final L of TROPICAL, leaving TROPICA, which 'Order' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a small orange stone fruit.

clue.text: Give wrong facts to girl when talking in class

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the word for a girl serves for the opening sound

parts.note: Miss is a title for a girl or young woman
a form is a school class in Britain

explanation.surface: Telling a pupil who chats during lessons something untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: MISS said aloud gives the sound of MIS; 'class' is a school form, as British schools call their year groups.
explanation.definitionFit: To misinform is to mislead someone with false information.

clue.text: Rough wit buoyant in the evening

indicators.note: something rough is not in finished shape, so the three letters of wit are knocked into a new order

parts.note: buoyant means floating, or light

explanation.surface: A coarse but cheerful sense of humour on display at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' is the anagram signal, not a description of the wit; 'in' is a link word between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Twilight is the dim light at dusk, the start of the evening.

clue.text: Carefully devised artesian idea dismissed

parts.note: an artesian well is a bore where water rises under pressure
an idea is a thought
a dismissed batsman in cricket is out

explanation.surface: A well-planned scheme for a water bore is rejected.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-thought-out describes a plan considered with care in every detail.

clue.text: Plant some to fill up in the garden

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are used, running together across them

explanation.surface: Instructions to plant enough to fill the flower beds.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant sits inside 'fill up in'; 'to' and 'the garden' are surface padding round it.
explanation.definitionFit: The lupin is a garden flower with tall spikes of blooms.

clue.text: Chapel by the sea

definitions.meaning: a porch or chapel at the west end of some English churches
the lake in northern Israel called a sea, where Jesus walked on water

explanation.walkthrough: 'by' links two senses: a church chapel, and the Sea of Galilee.
explanation.definitionFit: A galilee is a church porch or chapel, and the Sea of Galilee is the lake of the Gospels.

clue.text: Barter interrupted by one in angry outburst

indicators.note: the word for barter is broken into by the letter for one

parts.note: to barter is to trade
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Haggling cut short when someone flies into a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' links wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long, furious speech of denunciation.

clue.text: Charming disposition prior to instructions for dismissal

indicators.note: the first piece comes before the second
a disposition is an arrangement, so the letters of the first word are set out in another order

parts.note: orders are instructions

explanation.surface: A pleasant temperament before being given commands to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposition' looks like temperament, but it means an arranging: CHARMING rearranged. 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Marching orders are a notice to go, as when someone is sacked or sent away.

clue.text: Streaks of cloud or steam with rail travel

indicators.note: the letters travel about, moving into new positions

explanation.surface: Wisps of smoke trailing from a steam train as it runs along the rails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'travel' shuffles STEAM and RAIL together; the surface makes the streaks smoke from the engine.
explanation.definitionFit: Mare's tails are long thin wisps of high cirrus cloud, likened to a horse's tail.

clue.text: Popular characters lack support in this region

indicators.note: the letters (characters) of the first word go without the letters of the second, the remainder being rearranged

parts.note: to support is to hold up, giving UP

explanation.surface: Well-liked people find no backing in a particular area.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the letters U and P out of POPULAR leaves P, O, L, A, R, which already read in order as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A polar region is the area around the North or South Pole.

clue.text: Using few words in study of people going without

indicators.note: the word for people goes round the outside of the word for study

parts.note: laic means lay people, the laity, as opposed to clergy
to con is an old word for to study or learn by heart

explanation.surface: Someone writes tersely in an essay about the deprived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going without' looks like poverty, but it is a container signal: the word for people goes outside the word for study.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic speech is terse and brief, after the Spartans of Laconia.

clue.text: Smack ushered in confusion

parts.note: a smack is a taste or flavour, a tang
to usher someone is to lead them, so ushered means led

explanation.surface: A slap delivered while guests are shown to their seats in a muddle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tangled is knotted and muddled, the state of disorder the definition describes.

clue.text: Small presentation?

parts.note: a presentation made small: the clipped, informal word for the act of presenting someone or opening a piece of music

explanation.definitionFit: The word is a clipped form of the longer word for a presentation or opening passage.

clue.text: Do I steal off to be out of the way?

indicators.note: off means wrong or awry, so these letters are put in another order

explanation.surface: A thief wonders whether to slip away to some quiet spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges the eight letters of DO I STEAL; 'to be' links them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An isolated place is remote and cut off, far from others.

clue.text: Cora happy to be involved in old books

indicators.note: letters that become involved are tangled together and reordered

explanation.surface: A cheerful woman named Cora enjoys antique volumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be involved' rearranges CORA HAPPY; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apocrypha are ancient biblical writings outside the accepted canon.

clue.text: Lady Emma's husband a poet?

parts.note: John Milton was the poet of Paradise Lost

explanation.surface: Was Nelson's mistress married to a writer of verse?
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Emma Hamilton was Nelson's mistress; her husband was Sir William, so 'Lady Emma's' names the family surname she took from him. The '?' admits the husband was no poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma, Lady Hamilton, took her married surname from her husband, the diplomat Sir William.

clue.text: Giant split in the City

parts.note: the legendary British giant whose name is shared between two carved figures in the City of London, as though one giant had been split into two

explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district; the figures Gog and Magog stand in its Guildhall.
explanation.definitionFit: Gogmagog is the legendary giant of British myth, later split into the pair Gog and Magog of the London Guildhall.

clue.text: Maiden in village play?

parts.note: a hamlet is a small village, so the play is Hamlet and the young woman is its tragic heroine

explanation.walkthrough: 'village' is a pun on Shakespeare's Hamlet, a hamlet being a small village.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophelia is the young woman in Hamlet who drowns after going mad.

clue.text: Writer in two languages? Yes!

parts.note: oui is French for yes
da is Russian for yes

explanation.surface: An author who works in two tongues answers enthusiastically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in two languages' tells you to say yes twice in foreign tongues: French then Russian. Ouida was the pen name of the Victorian novelist Maria Louise Ramé.
explanation.definitionFit: Ouida was a Victorian novelist, author of Under Two Flags.

clue.text: Chilling conditions reported for elusive monster

indicators.note: a report of a sighting, spoken aloud, gives the sound of the word

parts.note: sighting the hard-to-spot Loch Ness monster, one would report 'I see Ness'

explanation.surface: Frosty weather is noted in a dispatch about Nessie.
explanation.walkthrough: The Loch Ness monster of Scotland is famously elusive, so spotting it you would say 'I see Ness', which sounds like the answer. 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Iciness is a state of freezing cold, a chilling condition.

clue.text: The Queen of Persia and her pages

definitions.meaning: the Jewish queen of the Persian king Ahasuerus in the Bible
the Old Testament book named after that queen

explanation.surface: A Persian royal and her young attendants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pages' suggests boy servants, but it means the pages of the biblical book that bears her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther was the biblical queen of Persia, and the Book of Esther tells her story.

clue.text: A planner — one having a go in Venice, for example

definitions.meaning: a plotter, someone who devises cunning plans

definitions.text: one having a go in Venice, for example
definitions.meaning: I (one) with A GO gives Iago, the plotter of Othello who works in Venice: an example of the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a pun: one (I) having A GO is IAGO, Shakespeare's villain in Venice, an example of a plotter.
explanation.definitionFit: A schemer is a plotter; Iago, the Venetian villain, is a classic example.

clue.text: Make a note of car miles

parts.note: the Mini is a classic small British car

explanation.surface: Jot down the mileage of your little car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a note' looks like an instruction to write, but 'a note' is the definition; 'Make' and 'of' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A minim is a musical note held for half a semibreve.

clue.text: Where lovers meet at Victoria and Waterloo?

definitions.text: Where lovers meet at Victoria and Waterloo?

parts.words: Where lovers meet at Victoria and Waterloo?
parts.note: journeys end in lovers meeting, as Shakespeare says, and Victoria and Waterloo are London rail stations where lines end

explanation.walkthrough: Victoria and Waterloo are London railway stations where the lines finish; 'journeys end in lovers meeting' is from Twelfth Night.
explanation.definitionFit: Termini are end stations of rail lines, the places journeys finish.

clue.text: Legendary beauty who captivated the French capital

definitions.text: Legendary beauty who captivated the French capital

parts.words: Legendary beauty who captivated the French capital
parts.note: the beauty of Greek legend who won the heart of the Trojan prince Paris, whose name is also the capital of France

explanation.walkthrough: The French capital is Paris; the Trojan prince Paris was captivated by this beauty and carried her off to Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen of Troy was the legendary beauty of Greek myth whose abduction started the Trojan War.

clue.text: Fit soldiers at wit's end for kit

parts.note: to fit out is to equip
soldiers are men, a crossword staple

indicators.note: the end of the word wit's is its last letter

explanation.surface: Troops who have run out of ideas need to be properly outfitted.
explanation.definitionFit: Equipment is the gear or outfit needed for a task, as kit is.

clue.text: Restore E Germany's military strength — it's furthest behind

parts.note: the prefix re- means again, as in restore
arms are military strength, giving ARM
E (east) in Germany's language is Ost

explanation.surface: A call to rebuild the East German army, which lags behind the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Restore ... military strength' reads as REARM, interrupted by 'E Germany's': east in German is OST. 'it's' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearmost means last in line, the one at the very back.

clue.text: Recognized standards supported by a churchman

parts.note: par is an accepted standard level, so pars are standards
something on another is supported by it

explanation.surface: Accepted norms are upheld by a member of the clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down-style reading PARS rests on ON; 'a' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A parson is a parish priest, a clergyman.
